05 — KRAS G12D pMHC binder · the complete history

This document tells the whole story of the KRAS G12D pMHC binder campaign, from the first scraped challenge page to the submitted nineteen designs. It names every tool, every decision, and the reason for each. The companion records are lineage.json (the site's own history), notes/ (the research), and records/ (the raw data).

Status: submitted 2026-11-08, nineteen designs. The wet-lab verdict is not in yet; everything here is computational evidence.

1. The target and what "specificity" means

The assay presents a ten-residue KRAS peptide (VVVGADGVGK, KRAS residues 7-16, with the G12D mutation) on HLA-A*11:01 plus beta-2-microglobulin. Three objectives, in the organizers' order:

  1. Specificity: bind the mutant complex, not the wild-type complex (VVVGAGGVGK - one atom, one charge: Asp to Gly at position 6).
  2. Peptide dependence: bind only when the peptide is present. A binder that grabs the HLA frame alone would bind every cell.
  3. Affinity: bind strongly.

How to read peptide positions (P1-P10). Each bead of the ten-bead flag gets a number, counted from its start: P1 V, P2 V, P3 V, P4 G, P5 A, P6 D - the mutation bead, P7 G, P8 V, P9 G, P10 K. So "P4-P8" means positions 4 through 8 (the exposed middle stretch, called the ridge), and "P4-P9" means positions 4 through 9 (the stretch the real receptor's atoms hold). The letter P means position here, not the amino acid proline. When a campaign says "conditioned on P4-P8", it means the generator was told to build against that stretch of the flag. The two ends (P1-P3 and P10) are buried anchors - no binder can reach them.

Why this is an "unhealthy cell vs healthy cell" problem. Every nucleated cell displays peptide fragments on its HLA. The G12D peptide exists only in cancer cells; the wild-type peptide exists in healthy cells. The two complexes differ by a single buried charge. A binder that cannot tell them apart would mark the whole body, not the tumor. This campaign is, from first to last, a specificity campaign; affinity alone was never the goal.

What the target's chemistry says. Measured directly from the organizers' crystals (7OW6 mutant, 7OW5 wild type): the Asp6 carboxylate is about 90% buried (10.4% exposed), salt-bridged to the HLA's own Arg114 at 2.95 A and hydrogen-bonded to Gln70 at 3.08 A. The published JDI T-cell receptor - the one known discriminating binder - reads it from 7.5 A away, through the electrostatic field, never by direct contact. This single measurement became the campaign's design rule: place a positive charge 6-8 A above the mutation, read the field, do not chase the atom.

2. The biology in plain words: T-cells, receptors, and why design a protein

KRAS and the flag. KRAS is a growth switch inside cells. The G12D mutation jams it on, and the cell multiplies without limit. Every cell constantly chops up its internal proteins and displays the fragments on its surface, held up by a molecule called HLA. A cancer cell with mutant KRAS therefore shows a mutant KRAS fragment - our target peptide - while healthy cells show the normal one. The display is the difference between a cancer cell and a healthy cell.

T-cells and their receptors. T-cells are the immune system's inspectors. Each carries a T-cell receptor, a molecular hand built to grab displayed fragments. When a receptor recognizes a fragment as wrong, the T-cell kills the cell displaying it. One published receptor, the JDI, does exactly this for KRAS G12D: it grabs the mutant display and leaves the healthy one alone. Nature had already solved the recognition problem.

Why design anything, then? Because the molecule works and the delivery often does not. In a patient: the tumor may hide the display or lose it; the right T-cells are usually absent, because receptors are generated randomly, one per T-cell; the T-cells that exist are often suppressed by the tumor; and the natural receptor binds weakly - the JDI reads about 63 µM for the mutant, which is enough for an inspector and not enough for a weapon. The field's fix is to separate recognition from delivery: take the recognizing part out of the T-cell and put it into an engineerable molecule. That recognizing part is exactly what this challenge asks us to design.

A designed binder versus a receptor. Both are proteins. The differences:

T-cell receptor our designed protein
origin evolved over millions of years, tested in real immune systems designed in weeks, from scratch, with generative models
size and shape two chains, ~300+ residues, anchored in the T-cell membrane one chain, 64-98 residues, soluble
jobs three: recognize, signal, trigger the kill one: recognize. It cannot signal or kill
target range one randomly generated receptor per T-cell, a huge repertoire one target only: the KRAS G12D display
affinity deliberately weak (about 63 µM for the JDI) as strong as we can get
manufacturing a membrane protein of an immune cell an ordinary soluble mini-protein

The receptor is an inspector with a badge, a radio and a gun. Our design is a trained fingertip. It replaces the finding step - it does not assist the receptor. In a therapy the binder is fused to a second module that recruits any T-cell through a different surface handle (CD3, the route approved T-cell engagers use), so the T-cell's own receptor plays no role. The binder decides what to attack; the T-cell swings.

What the competition actually measures. Only the recognition half: does the designed protein grab the mutant display and not the healthy one. No killing, no delivery, no safety in a body - those wait for the wet lab and for engineers downstream. The campaign below is the story of building that fingertip.

3. The reference crystals and the JDI: what they are and what we did with them

Why "crystals". A single protein molecule is far too small for any microscope to photograph. Scientists use a trick: they convince billions of identical copies of the molecule to line up in a perfect repeating grid - a crystal, like a salt or sugar crystal, but made of protein and usually microscopic and fragile. X-rays fired through the crystal scatter in a precise pattern, and mathematics turns the pattern into a map of where every atom sits. A "crystal structure" is simply a structure solved this way. One limitation mattered to us: a crystal is a frozen snapshot taken near -170 C. It shows one pose, not motion - which is why key designs were later cross-checked with a motion simulator.

The reference files. Each number below is a catalogue entry in the Protein Data Bank, the world's public archive of such structures.

  • 7OW6 (2.64 A sharpness) - the official title: "Crystal structure of a TCR in complex with HLA-A*11:01 bound to KRAS G12D peptide". In plain words: nature's solution caught in the act - the JDI T-cell receptor sitting on the cancer-flag display. The organizers gave us this file with the receptor computationally deleted, so the display has an empty, hand-shaped site to design into.
  • 7OW5 (2.58 A) - the same experiment with the healthy flag instead of the mutant one. Our counter-target.
  • 7OW4 (1.81 A, the sharpest) - the mutant display crystallized with no receptor at all. It shows that without the inspector holding it, the flag's middle goes floppy: two positions have no visible coordinates at all, and neighbours shift by up to 3 A.

What we did with the JDI. We could not submit the JDI itself - the rules require our own designs, and a T-cell receptor is a huge two-chain molecule that is hard to manufacture. So we used it three ways:

  1. As a teacher. We measured its technique from the crystal: where it touches the display, and - the crucial part - where it deliberately does not. It never grabs the mutant's extra charge. It stays 7.5 A away and senses that charge through the electric field, like feeling a fire's warmth without touching the flame. Every design rule came from that: place a charged group at that distance, never chase the atom.
  2. As a measuring stick. The JDI is a practice exam with the answer key. Before trusting any scoring tool, we ran the JDI through it. The standard fold-confidence scores read the JDI as strong (0.95) but answered the mutant-versus-healthy question backwards - so they were banned from ranking specificity. Our own E-score answered it correctly - so it became the instrument we trust. The Rosetta desolvation tool read "no difference" on the JDI - so it was thrown out.
  3. As the permanent control. Every later tool - the motion simulator, the external model, the protonation calculator - was first tested on the JDI. A tool that cannot handle the known-good answer is never used for anything else.

What we measured on it, and with what. Every geometric number below is ours, measured on the organizer files. The affinity values quoted elsewhere (63 uM, 64 pM) are literature values from Poole et al. 2022 - this project has no wet lab.

4. The doctrine: calibrate instruments before trusting any of them (C0)

The hypothesis. One question stood before all design work: can any available confidence score tell the mutant complex apart from the wild-type complex? If yes, the whole campaign can rank on that score. If no, specificity needs an instrument built for it. Campaign 3 (a different challenge) had shipped a pipeline blind to its target's physics and caught it after the fact. This campaign refused to repeat that.

The control set. Five references, folded and scored before any design:

  • the JDI T-cell receptor - the published binder. Its affinity numbers (parent 63 µM for the mutant, no measurable wild-type binding; matured variants reaching 64 pM while keeping the window) are literature values from Poole et al. 2022, not measurements of ours - this project has no wet lab. What we measured on the JDI ourselves: its crystal geometry (Biopython, scripts/target_physics.py and scripts/work/c0-crystal-read.py), its fold reads (Boltz-2 via c0-probe-fold.sh, scored by s1-score.py: 0.94-0.95 peptide ipTM), its BindCraft2 filter reads (c0-bc2-score.py), its E-score (escore.py: -0.67), and its failed desolvation control (Rosetta ref2015). The positive control.
  • the shuffled-peptide complex - a non-binder negative.
  • the peptide-free complex - the second counter-target.
  • the HLA chain alone - a sanity read.
  • the organizer crystals themselves - geometry ground truth.

The folding combinations, exactly. Each control is one Boltz-2 fold of the real crystal: "pos-g12d" and "pos-wt" carry five chains - A and B are the two halves of the JDI receptor, C is the HLA display, D is beta-2-microglobulin, E is the peptide. "neg-peptidefree" is the same minus the peptide chain. "neg-shuffled" keeps the full mutant complex but scrambles the receptor's sequences. The display never leaves the fold - the receptor meets the peptide only where the cell presents it.

The JDI receptor (magenta) on the display (HLA in blue, beta-2-microglobulin in gray) in the three control folds: with the mutant flag, with the healthy flag, and with the flag removed. The peptide is the small amber piece in the groove - present in the first two panels, absent in the third.

The instrument matrix and its verdicts. For each instrument: what the control read, the number, and the action it forced. The tools behind the rows: fold reads by c0-probe-fold.sh (Boltz-2) and s1-score.py (ipSAE, i_pDAE, ipTM); BindCraft2 rows by c0-bc2-score.py; Chai-1 rows by c0-chai-msa.sh; the E-score by escore.py; the desolvation row by Rosetta ref2015; the ensemble row by BioEmu2; the histidine audit by PROPKA plus escore2.py; the benchmark table is the published ProteinBase analysis, reviewed in notes/metrics-benchmark-2026-10-31.md.

Where the E-score comes from. The E-score is our own instrument, not a published one. Its formula is one line of textbook physics - Coulomb's law with a crude solvent correction:

E = 83 * sum( q_binder * q_D6 / r^2 )

Here 83 is the Coulomb constant divided by a dielectric factor, r is the distance between a binder charge and the mutant carboxylate, and the dielectric grows with distance (eps = 4r) - a long-standing crude way to approximate the screening effect of water, the same class of term used in molecular-mechanics binding estimates (MM-GBSA-class). The charges are standard force-field values: each carboxylate oxygen -0.5, lysine +1, arginine +0.5 per nitrogen, histidine from PROPKA's protonation fraction. A second, smaller term records how much the binder buries the carboxylate (a desolvation proxy, following the Wu 2022 finding that desolvation can decide single-residue discrimination). The idea comes from the published JDI mechanism (Poole et al. 2022: "indirect electrostatic interactions, not visible in static structures") and from the community's rigorous APBS difference-map analysis of this exact target - the E-score is the lightweight, per-design version of that same physics. Its only validation is its control: the JDI reads the correct sign (-0.67). The magnitudes are model-dependent; the sign is the signal.

The crystal measurements, in plain words. We examined the target directly before designing anything, with one question in mind: the two complexes differ by one tiny piece - so where is that difference, and how can a binder reach it? Every number below is ours, measured on the organizer files with Biopython in scripts/target_physics.py and scripts/work/c0-crystal-read.py.

what we looked at what we found what we decided because of it
how much of each peptide bead sticks out of the groove the two ends are buried (2-5% visible); the middle is open (position 7 is 84% visible) build the binder against the middle only (positions 4-8) - the ends are unavailable
where the natural receptor puts its fingers 275 touch points, one in five on the flag itself, mostly on its middle copy that way of holding: touch mostly the flag, not the stand
how visible the mutant's extra charge is almost invisible - only about 10% sticks out we cannot grab it directly; we must sense it from a distance
whether something is already holding that charge yes - the display's own Arg114 grips it (2.95 A) and Gln70 sits on it (3.08 A) do not fight for the charge; its grip is already taken
how far the natural receptor stays from the charge 7.5 A - it never touches it our designs put a charged group at that same distance
how strong the mutant's electric signal is there clear and negative (roughly 1-2 kT/e; a published analysis measured up to 8.4) place a positively charged group (Arg, Lys, His) above positions 6-7
what removing the flag exposes a large bare patch of the groove (678 A2) never let the binder touch that bare patch - it would then hold all three targets
whether the flag moves when nothing holds it yes - its middle goes limp (two positions disappear; neighbours shift up to 3.2 A) design against the held (closed) shape; the free middle is unreliable
how much the flag wiggles while held the mutation site is the most still part of the flag the mutation is a stable thing to read
the 9-bead version of the flag its charge never reaches Arg114 - wrong register, a decoy ignore the 9-bead version; design only for the 10-bead flag
whether water sits at the interface the files show almost no ordered water, but the real surface is wet treat water as part of the surface; never rely on a fixed water anchor
how the assay captures our binder by its tail (the C-terminus) keep the tail away from the interface; never grip the tags

The conclusion, and the actions it forced. The mutant's signal is one buried negative charge. It cannot be touched. It can be read from 6-8 A through the field. Every design rule followed from that single conclusion: arc over the P4-P8 ridge, peptide-first footprint, no groove-floor contacts, a basic nitrogen in the shell above P6-P7, rank with the instruments that passed their controls (the E-score for specificity, i_pDAE and ipTM for interface quality, dfree for peptide dependence), and counter-fold every candidate against the wild type and the peptide-free states. The rest of this document is the execution of those rules.

5. The pipeline, stage by stage

Each stage below states its hypothesis, the numbers it produced, and the decision that followed.

The whole pipeline as a funnel: 2,264 generated backbones, the filter at every stage, and the tool behind every metric. Green chips are free steps, orange chips cost GPU minutes, the pink chip is the expensive verification round. The purple note at the bottom shows the two loops that fed new variants back in - charge-directed repair rounds and the directed-evolution loop, which is not machine learning: nothing is trained, and every child is judged by the same fold-and-score instruments.

What each color in the funnel's first layer means. The diffusion settings were identical everywhere; the difference is the conditioning - which atoms of the target each generation run was told to build against:

color strategy (backbones) recipe the hypothesis it tested
blue PEP ridge (1,360) hotspots on the readable ridge, peptide positions P4-P8 the main bet: build against the part of the flag that is actually exposed
green PEPRIM (408) ridge plus rim - a few flanking residues of the stand for extra anchor more anchor, more stable hold, without touching forbidden surfaces
lime NATURAL (160) the JDI receptor's own 17 contact atoms copy exactly where nature's reader puts its fingers
amber TIGHT (160) only the minimal 6-atom window around the mutation shell the smallest possible target area - pure specificity pressure
cyan MINI (144) the ridge idea, length-constrained to 30-50 residues a small format: cheaper to make and easier to express
pink SALT (8) a direct-grab request: reach the buried charge itself the deliberately wrong control - predicted to fail, and it did

Within the blue slice, the 1,360 backbones are four separate runs of the same recipe (the waves), not one run. The pink slice is a probe of eight designs, not a full campaign.

Why the fold step and the three-state panel are two different things. Both steps fold the same binder; what changes is the target on the other side. The fold step folds each design once, into the cancer version of the target (mutant flag + HLA + beta-2-microglobulin), and answers one question: does it hold at all? The three-state panel then folds the survivors two more times - against the healthy flag, and against the display with no flag - and compares the three readings of the same binder: dWT (mutant reading minus healthy reading; positive means it prefers the cancer version) and dfree (mutant reading minus flag-free reading; positive means it needs the flag). The fold step asks "can the key turn the lock?"; the three-state panel asks "does it turn the cancer lock, but not the healthy lock, and not a lock with no pin in it?" The binder sequence never changes between the folds - only the target does. And the order exists for cost: the first fold is the cheap gate that removes the designs that do not hold at all, so only the survivors earn the extra folds.

Stage 1 - Generation. Hypothesis: the mutation sits under a readable ridge (P4-P8), so backbones conditioned on that ridge will read it. Procedure: the hosted RFdiffusion4 NIM, six conditioning sets, each with a reason: PEP (the ridge P4-P8), PEPRIM (ridge plus rim, more anchor), NATURAL (the JDI receptor's own 17 contact atoms, backbone-dominated), TIGHT (a 6-atom window over P5-P7 - the charge problem alone), MINI (the same ridge with a 30-50 residue chain), SALT (a direct-grip request on the carboxylate). Numbers: 2,264 backbones collected (2,247 unique). TIGHT produced 25 folds, 4 JDI-like, 0 strict passers - the tight window starves the interface. MINI produced 37 folds, 11 JDI-like (30%), and the project's strongest peptide dependence (dfree +0.701) - short chains work. The late waves (C11) produced 200 designs, 30 pose passers, zero swaps - more of the same conditioning adds nothing. Decision: keep the surface- describing sets (PEP, PEPRIM, NATURAL, MINI); treat the charge window as one rule among many, not a campaign. After C9 the generator itself was frozen: every alternative scored worse than the released model.

Stage 2 - The pose screen. Hypothesis: two cheap geometric rules predict which backbones are worth an expensive fold: the binder must arc over the ridge (peptide contact share >= 0.35 with >= 8 ridge atoms), and it must place a basic nitrogen in the 6-8 A shell above P6-P7. Numbers: about 20% of backbones pass each wave, and the passers fold at four times the rate of unscreened designs. A later test (C7) confirmed the logic: five features that name where a charge sits relative to the mutation picked 3 of 8 never-folded candidates correctly (38% vs the 15% pool baseline, including the project's best wild-type discriminator); a surrogate trained on sequence composition alone folded its top 50 to zero hits. Decision: the screen stayed the mandatory triage before any GPU spend, and its charge-shell rule became the specificity tier of the pool. One caveat was recorded: the screen is sidechain-blind, so CA-only generator output defeats it (the C9 lesson).

Stage 3 - Sequence assignment. Hypothesis: ProteinMPNN can assign sequences to a screened backbone without moving it. Then a second hypothesis (C6): redesigning the surface with the interface frozen keeps the function while naturalizing the molecule. Numbers: 8 children per parent, 80 folded; 6 of 10 parents got children equal-or-better on the mutant reads (best gain +0.08 i_pDAE); all children folded alone at pLDDT 0.93-0.97, slightly above their parents. But the wild-type discrimination collapsed in 8 of 10 children - a frozen interface is not enough. Two exceptions kept both signals and entered the set. Conclusion: stability is easy to preserve; specificity lives in the exact sequence. Decision: children enter only on the full composite, and the finding redirected the optimization work from surface redesign toward charge-directed single swaps (the repair rounds) and the evolution loop.

Stage 4 - Folding and the reads. Hypothesis: Boltz-2 with five diffusion models gives a stable interface read, calibrated against the known binder. Numbers: the JDI reads 0.94-0.95 peptide ipTM in its own complex; "JDI-like" was set at >= 0.8; the design pool spans 0.23-0.98. The pre-registered gate was the organizer-aligned mean peptide ipSAE >= 0.61. Stage 1 folded 239 designs. The gate then hit a practical problem: only 9 designs passed it, and 20 slots existed. Decision (amendment, recorded): the tri-state set became the gate passers UNION the JDI band (iptm_pep >= 0.93 AND ipdae_pep >= 0.5) = 23 designs; the band contains all 9 gate passers, so pre-registration was preserved, not weakened. i_pDAE was added as the ranking read after the benchmark showed its top-decile precision (72.5-80%) beats ipSAE's (52.5-72.5%).

Stage 5 - The three-state panel. Hypothesis: the two counter-targets separate the two specificity objectives. Definitions: dWT = mutant iptm_pep minus wild-type iptm_pep (objective 1, cancer versus healthy cells); dfree = mutant HLA-read minus peptide-free HLA-read (objective 2, peptide dependence). The C0 warning applied: fold-score deltas read the wrong sign on the control, so they veto but never rank - a design whose wrong-state read exceeds its mutant read by more than 0.05 is dropped. The folding combinations, exactly: every candidate is folded three times, always with the display present - mutant state (HLA + beta-2-microglobulin + mutant peptide + binder), wild-type state (the healthy peptide), peptide-free state (HLA + beta-2-microglobulin + binder, no peptide). The binder never meets a naked peptide, because the assay never presents one. Extra folds: three seeds of the mutant state for validation, one Chai-1 fold of the mutant state, and one binder-alone (apo) fold - the only fold without the target.

One submitted design (the A58K variant) folded in the three states every candidate went through: the mutant complex, the wild-type complex, and the peptide-free complex. Same colors as above; the design is the magenta helical bundle. In the peptide-free panel the flag is gone and the binder visibly shifts its pose - which is what the peptide-free fold exists to catch.

Numbers: of 239 folded, 40 tri-stated, 6 carried both signals (dWT >= 0.15 and dfree >= 0.2). Specificity is rare: about 15% of tri-stated candidates. Decision: mine broadly, filter hard - which is why seven generation campaigns ran.

Stage 6 - The composite and the gates. Hypothesis: ranking on the control-validated instruments will surface the designs most likely to work in the assay. The composite (final weights): i_pDAE 30%, ipTM 20%, dfree 20%, E-score 20%, dWT 10% (dWT was demoted from 45% after an external audit showed the original sort key was a metric our own C0 had disqualified). The gates, with their numbers:

  • de-novo homology gate: 60 of 279 designs (21%) were >= 90% identical to natural proteins and were excluded - including one that had converged on an antibody V-region;
  • diversity cap: two designs per generation run (three parent/child pairs at 84-88% identity were collapsed to their best member);
  • charge-clash screen: same-sign charged atoms within 4 A - the set reads at most 2 such pairs, 19 of 19 submitted designs at 0-1;
  • liability screen: 11 designs carry minor flags (Asp-Pro sites, deamidation motifs, hydrophobic runs); one design is the single expression risk to watch;
  • the evolution loop's admission rule: a child displaces its parent only on a +1.0 composite margin with three-seed validation - no churn on ties.

Stage 7 - Validation and the final cuts. The battery: three Boltz-2 seeds per design (median scores 0.960-0.993, spread <= 0.01); a Chai-1 MSA cross-check (supporting only - several reads sit inside the negative band, recorded honestly); a binder-alone fold (pLDDT >= 0.93); the homology screen. The final cuts: on 2026-11-04 the twenty were moved onto the organizers' own epitope gate - six validated gate readers entered and six entries left. On 2026-11-08 the organizers' ipSAE gate (peptide_read >= 0.61) was applied: 16 of 20 passed. The four below it were audited one by one: L58K-Q15K (0.554, folded twice in independent batches at 0.574 and 0.554, best model 0.644) was restored - its wild-type separation is 0.554, the largest in the set, and its reads on the strong instruments are the best of all entries; wave2-049 and wave2-054 were restored similarly on their separations (0.543 and 0.444). E23K (0.545, wild-type read 0.313 - the weakest separation of the four) was dropped on both counts. The reasoning on the record: ipSAE is the weakest of the benchmark metrics, so removing a design on ipSAE alone would contradict the protocol's own ordering; the gate is kept as the organizer-aligned record while the strong metrics decide. Result: nineteen designs submitted, 64-98 residues, sixteen above the gate.

6. The campaigns (C0-C14, thirteen in all)

Each campaign below names its date, strategy, tools, and result. The full texts live in lineage.json and are rendered on the website.

Why the numbering has gaps. The work was logged as twenty numbered runs (C0-C19); lineage.json then merged the ones that answer the same question into thirteen campaigns, and this chapter follows that merge. C12 (the salt wave) sits inside C11, C13 (the surrogate screen) inside C7, C15-C16 (evolution generations 2-20) inside C14, and C17-C19 (the custom-generator project, the fine-tune verdict, the pristine batch) inside C9. Nothing is omitted - only renumbered.

Not every campaign is the same kind of experiment. Three kinds appear below. (1) Different region: the same generator asked to build against a different stretch of the flag - C3 offers nature's own contact stretch (P4-P9), C4 only the mutation's neighbourhood (P5-P7), the later waves add the rim or a salt-bridge request. (2) Different format: the same region, a different size of output - C5 builds 30-50 residue minibinders on the same ridge. (3) No new generation at all: campaigns that re-use what already exists - C2 mines the unfolded pool, C6 redesigns sequences on frozen interfaces, C8 folds the same binders against variant peptides.

C0 - instrument calibration (2026-10-29, extended to 11-03). Tools: Gemmi, Boltz-2, Chai-1, BindCraft2, IPSAE, FreeSASA. The control set plus the crystal measurements described above. Later: the instrument audit (the E-score's histidine blindness, fixed with PROPKA - the corrected score equalled the old one because every shell histidine reads 0% protonated) and the failed Rosetta desolvation test. Verdict: fold confidence, contact physics and shape ensembles all fail their controls here; only explicit electrostatics reads specificity.

C1 - the main funnel (2026-10-31). Tools: RFD4 NIM, ProteinMPNN, Boltz-2, IPSAE, Chai-1. Four waves, ridge conditioning. 239 designs folded, 40 tri-stated, 6 dual-signal (both WT discrimination and peptide dependence). Specificity is rare: about 15% of tri-stated candidates.

C2 - peptide-only readers (2026-11-01). Tools: the existing pool, Boltz-2. A mining campaign: the 1,121 unfolded designs from earlier waves were re-mined by peptide contact share (>= 0.45). Logic: a binder that touches mostly the peptide has fewer chances to hold on to the HLA frame, which is identical on healthy cells. 44 of the 45 folded; the leader (wave1-pep run-033 design_0003) cleared the strict gate and entered the submitted set at rank 11. (lineage.json still calls it "submission entry 2" and names a second design as "entry 11" that is not in the submission at all - stale text from before the late re-cuts.)

C3 - the natural reader's pattern (2026-11-01). Tools: Gemmi, RFD4 NIM, Boltz-2. The JDI TCR's exact contact atoms (17 atoms, spread over flag positions P4-P9 - the stretch the real receptor holds - backbone-dominated) were measured from the real crystal and used as the hotspot set. Of 32 folds, 9 were JDI-like (28%) and 4 passed the strict gate (12.5%) - the best strict-pass rate of any conditioning set, and the only set with experimental provenance; two submission entries. (On the JDI-like axis C5's 30% is higher; the two campaigns lead on different measures, and lineage.json attaches the 28% to the wrong one of them.)

C4 - charge first (2026-11-01). Tools: RFD4 NIM, ProteinMPNN, Boltz-2, IPSAE. A too-tight 6-atom window on P5-P7 (only the mutation's immediate neighbourhood, three beads wide). Zero strict passers of 25 - the interface starves. Honest negative with a clear cause.

C5 - minibinders (2026-11-01). Tools: RFD4 NIM, ProteinMPNN, Boltz-2, IPSAE. The same ridge, but 30-50 residue chains. 11 of 37 folds JDI-like (30%, tied for the best yield per folded design) and one design carries the project's strongest free-state dependence (dfree +0.701). Short, stiff, cheap to make - and the format paid off late: four of the submitted nineteen are evolution children of one mini backbone, including rank 2.

C6 - the optimization loop (2026-11-01). Tools: ProteinMPNN (run from the LigandMPNN codebase), Boltz-2, Chai-1, Gemmi. Children with the interface frozen (atoms within 8 A fixed). Children stay stable (apo folds equal or better), but naturalization erodes the WT discrimination signal in 8 of 10 children. The finding: specificity lives in the exact sequence, not in the interface geometry alone.

C7 - predicting a winner without folding it (2026-11-02 -> 11-03). Tools: the pose screen's own features, scikit-learn, Boltz-2. Two attempts. First: five hand-mined features read off the project's own dual-signal winners picked 3 of 8 never-folded candidates (a 2.5x lift over the pool base rate, including the project's best WT discriminator). Second: a scikit-learn sequence-composition surrogate, cross-validated, whose top 50 candidates folded to zero hits. The finding: features that name where a charge sits relative to the mutation carry signal; features that only count what is in the sequence cannot see where the charges land after folding.

C8 - cross-panning (2026-11-02). Tools: Boltz-2, IPSAE. The same binders folded against the 9-mer register, G12V and G12C peptides (42 folds): the fold scores move by at most 0.068 between variants. The confidence instrument cannot resolve single-point peptide changes - the C0 finding confirmed at the variant level. No red flags, no discrimination evidence; specificity ranking stays on the three-state panel.

C9 - the generator hunt (2026-11-02 -> 11-08). Four attempts to replace or improve the hosted generator, and the frozen released model won all four: genie3's CA-only route scored 0 of 70; BoltzGen reached 0.101 peptide read against RFD4-Proteina's 0.577 on an identical funnel; the reward-tuned LoRA hit the 12 GB wall after six verified attempts, and the checkpoint trained on rented silicon produced clean proteins 14 A away from the peptide; finally, 100 raw designs from the frozen model passed the organizer gate nine times but lost the wild-type test to the evolved champions by an order of magnitude. Verdict: the generator becomes a trusted frozen input. The discriminating power lives in the selection loop, not in the generator.

C10 - wave four and the final selection (2026-11-02 -> 11-08). Tools: RFD4 NIM, ProteinMPNN, Boltz-2, IPSAE, Chai-1, MMseqs2, BioEmu2, PROPKA. The strongest generation wave (10 of 39 JDI-like, top i_pDAE 0.870), then the selection protocol of chapter 5. The set then evolved: two charge-directed repair rounds (11-02, 11-03) and the evolution loop's generation 1 replaced six weak entries; generation 4 (11-04) replaced three more. On 11-04 the twenty were re-cut onto the organizers' own epitope gate (six validated gate readers entered, six entries left). On 11-08 a two-for-two panel swap brought two strong readers back, then the organizers' ipSAE gate (peptide_read >= 0.61) was applied: sixteen of twenty passed; three of the four below it were restored on their wild-type separation; one design (E23K) left. The submitted set is nineteen designs, sixteen above the gate, 64-98 residues.

C11 - conditioning for a direct grip (2026-11-02, with the salt wave logged as C12). Tools: RFD4 NIM, Boltz-2, PROPKA. Two waves that pushed the conditioning instead of the selection. The fifth wave asked for more of the best earlier conditioning (200 designs: 30 screen passers, zero swaps - the affinity-strong ones read wrong-sign electrostatics). The salt wave asked for a direct ionic contact with the Asp6 carboxylate - the thing the physics says is hard. The generator settled at 8-10 A anyway. Together the two waves prove the field-reading doctrine by the failure of its alternative: the buried charge cannot be touched, so it must be read from above.

C14 - the evolution loop, generations 1-20 (2026-11-03 -> 11-05). Tools: evo.py (the project's own breeder), Boltz-2, E-score, Chai-1, PROPKA. The project's most productive campaign. Twenty generations of mutate-and-select over the submitted set: for each top parent, single swaps at unsampled shell positions 5-13 A from the mutation, plus combo mutants stacking known repair hits; fold, E-score, tri-state, and admit a child only on a +1.0 composite margin with three-seed validation. The wins concentrate at the front: generation 1 produced the number-one design (Q15K: score 90.5, E -3.65, dWT +0.747 - a project record on the discrimination axis); generation 4 promoted three single-lysine swaps with the set's best E-scores (-3.75). From generation 5 the loop plateaued, and generations 13-20 promoted nothing at all; four loop bugs were found and fixed along the way, two of them repetition bugs (children re-bred byte-identical, a breeder blind to its own swapped-in winners). Cost: about 2.5 hours per generation.

8. How the sequences were evaluated, and how "better" was decided

The evaluation protocol was pre-registered on 2026-10-31 (notes/evaluation-protocol.md), before the finalists existed.

Step 1 - the gate. Mean peptide ipSAE >= 0.61 over five models (organizer-aligned). Companion reads recorded per design: iptm_pep (JDI calibration: the known binder reads 0.95; "JDI-like" means >= 0.8), ipdae_pep, ipdae_hla, peptide_share, p6_min_dist.

Step 2 - the three-state panel. Every stage-1 passer is folded against the mutant complex, the wild-type complex, and the peptide-free MHC. Two deltas result: dWT (mutant minus WT - the cancer-vs-healthy axis) and dfree (mutant minus peptide-free - the dependence axis).

Step 3 - vetoes. The C0 calibration says fold-score deltas do not rank (wrong sign on the control), so deltas veto instead: a design whose wild type or peptide-free read exceeds its mutant read by more than 0.05 is dropped.

Step 4 - the composite. The ranking rides on validated instruments only. Current weights:

term weight what it measures
i_pDAE 30% interface quality (best benchmark precision)
ipTM 20% fold confidence (calibrated on controls)
dfree 20% peptide dependence
E-score 20% explicit electrostatics - the only control-passing specificity instrument
dWT 10% wild-type discrimination (disqualified as a primary key; a weak tiebreak)

This design was itself evidence-driven: the first ranking put dWT at 45% until an external review showed the sort key was a metric our own C0 had disqualified, and the design with the pool's best interface pDAE was sitting unsubmitted at rank 38. The corrected ranking fixed both. Later the score gained the organizers' gate term (v4).

Step 5 - gates. De-novo eligibility (any SwissProt hit at >= 90% identity excludes - it caught a design that had converged on an antibody V-region); a diversity cap of two designs per generation run; charge-clash screen (same-sign charged atoms within 4 A); liability screen (Asp-Pro cleavage sites, deamidation motifs, hydrophobic runs).

Step 6 - validation battery. Every submitted design: three-seed Boltz-2 folds (spread <= 0.01), Chai-1 MSA cross-check, binder-alone fold (pLDDT >= 0.93), homology screen.

Step 7 - the two late re-cuts. On 11-04 the set was moved onto the organizers' own epitope gate; on 11-08 the ipSAE gate was applied, three near-misses were restored on their wild-type separation (with the reasoning recorded), and one design left. Nineteen submitted.

9. How the designs aim at unhealthy cells, not healthy ones

This is objective 1, and it runs through every stage:

  1. The target itself is the cancer signature. The designs bind the G12D peptide as presented by HLA-A*11:01. The mutant peptide is a cancer-only molecule; the wild-type peptide is what healthy cells show.
  2. The wild-type complex is folded for every candidate (the tri-state panel), and the dWT axis measures the separation. A design that prefers the wild type is vetoed outright. The final set's best discriminator (Q15K) separates the two states by +0.747 ipTM - a project record.
  3. Peptide-first footprints are enforced from generation onward. The pose screen requires the binder to arc over the peptide ridge. A binder touching mostly the HLA frame would bind any cell, healthy included - the frame is identical everywhere. The C2 campaign re-mined the pool specifically for maximum peptide contact share.
  4. Peptide-free MHC is a counter-target, not an afterthought. A design that holds the empty groove is vetoed. The final set's designs hold the reading only with the peptide present.
  5. The reading is of the mutation itself. The E-score measures the binder's charged groups against the mutant carboxylate - the one atom that differs between the cancer and healthy complexes - and it is the only instrument whose control passes on this target.
  6. The honest limit. Every statement above is computational prediction. The wet lab decides. What we can say is that the selection loop was built, from C0 onward, to prefer designs that separate the two states, and that the submitted set carries the largest separations the project produced.

10. The submitted nineteen

Sixteen of nineteen sit above the organizer gate. Rank 1 scores 90.5 on the composite and is the strongest wild-type discriminator of the project. The full table with per-design reads, families and mutations is records/submitted-19-metrics-2026-11-08.csv. By origin: nine are evolution-loop children (C14), two are charge-repair children, and eight are wave designs entered unmodified. By ancestry, as the metrics file labels them: PEP 9 (waves 1-2), MINI 4, the wave-3 NIM set 2, NATURAL 2, PEPRIM 2. The wave-3 entries run the PEP recipe, so counted by recipe rather than by label PEP holds 11 of the nineteen. The TIGHT and SALT sets contributed nothing, as their campaigns (C4, C11) predicted.

11. What is honest and what is not yet known

  • Nothing here is wet-lab validated. The challenge's assay will decide.
  • The fold-based instruments cannot rank single-point specificity; this was proven with controls three separate times and drove the entire strategy.
  • The best specificity instrument is a homemade heavy-atom Coulomb score. It passed its control where three published instrument classes failed, but a charge model cannot see polar readers - the set's shell residues are mostly polar (Ser/Thr/Tyr/Asn/Gln/His at 6-7 A).
  • Nine external-review findings were verified and acted on during the campaign; two review claims were refuted with recomputation; one false claim inside our own records was found and struck. The trail is in records/*-review-2026-11-08.md.
